proofs.proof_tex:
Fix a feasible family \(f=(f_{a,z})\).  By the obstacle-set definition,
\[
0\leq f_{a,z}(r)\leq u_{a,z}(r)\qquad(a\in\mathcal A,\ z\in\mathcal Z,\ r\in[0,1]).
\]
Consequently the completion probability in the armwise completion definition is well defined and satisfies
\[
q_{a,z}(r)=\frac{f_{a,z}(r)}{u_{a,z}(r)}\in[0,1]
\quad\hbox{if }u_{a,z}(r)>0.
\]
If \(u_{a,z}(r)=0\), the same obstacle inequality forces \(f_{a,z}(r)=0\), and the stipulated value \(q_{a,z}(r)=0\) again gives
\[
q_{a,z}(r)u_{a,z}(r)=f_{a,z}(r).                                      \qquad\text{(1)}
\]
The piecewise ratio is Borel measurable because \(f_{a,z}\) and \(u_{a,z}\) are continuous and \(\{u_{a,z}>0\}\) is open.

We next verify the observation map event by event.  Write \((\widetilde T_a,\Delta_a)\) for the arm-\(a\) draw in the construction.  When \(\Delta_a=0\), the construction gives
\[
T(a)=\widetilde T_a\leq t_{\max}<t_{\max}+1=C(a),
\]
so
\[
\min\{T(a),C(a)\}=\widetilde T_a,
\qquad \mathbf 1\{C(a)\leq T(a)\}=0=\Delta_a.                         \qquad\text{(2)}
\]
When \(\Delta_a=1\), it gives \(C(a)=\widetilde T_a\) and \(T(a)\in\{\widetilde T_a,t_{\max}\}\).  Since \(0\leq\widetilde T_a\leq t_{\max}\),
\[
\min\{T(a),C(a)\}=\widetilde T_a,
\qquad \mathbf 1\{C(a)\leq T(a)\}=1=\Delta_a.                         \qquad\text{(3)}
\]
The weak inequality in (3) is precisely where the stipulated tie-as-dropout convention is used.  Equations (2)--(3), the observed marginal law of \(X\) used by the completion, the observed conditional kernel of \((\widetilde T_a,\Delta_a)\) given \(A=a,X\), and the protocol probabilities \(\pi_a(X)\) show that the observation map under \(P^f\) has law \(P_{\mathrm{obs}}\).  In particular, the law of the observed censoring record \((\widetilde T,\Delta)\), conditionally and marginally, is preserved.

The Bernoulli completion coin is conditionally independent of \((\widetilde T_a,\Delta_a)\) given \(X=(z,r)\), and its success probability is \(q_{a,z}(r)\).  Treatment is drawn only after the two potential arm records and independently of them given \(X\).  Therefore, using randomization and the dropout-capacity definition,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&E_{P^f}[(T(a)-\widetilde T)\Delta\mid A=a,Z=z,R=r]\\
&\quad=q_{a,z}(r)
E_{P_{\mathrm{obs}}}[(t_{\max}-\widetilde T)\Delta
 \mid A=a,Z=z,R=r]\\
&\quad=q_{a,z}(r)u_{a,z}(r)
=f_{a,z}(r),                                                            \qquad\text{(4)}
\end{aligned}
\]
where the final equality includes both the positive-capacity and zero-capacity cases by (1).  Thus the residual-contribution definition gives \(s^{P^f}_{a,z}=f_{a,z}\).

It remains to check membership rather than merely observational equivalence.  Defining realized \((T,C)=(T(A),C(A))\) gives consistency.  Drawing \(A\) independently of all potential arm records conditional on \(X\) gives the stated randomization property.  Equations (2)--(3) and the support of the observed record give \(0\leq T(a)\leq t_{\max}\).  All treatment-overlap, censoring-overlap, profile-mass, score-density, and observed-law H\"older conditions are inherited from the unchanged observed law.  Finally, (4) identifies the residual functions with \(f_{a,z}\), which are nonnegative, nondecreasing, and \(L\)-Lipschitz by feasibility.  These are exactly the membership conditions in the compatible-law definition.  Hence \(P^f\in\mathcal F(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\), with the claimed residual contribution and preserved observed censoring law.

Define the causal identified set, without reference to the proposed observed-law functional, by
\[
\Theta_I(P_{\mathrm{obs}})
:=\{\tau^P:P\in\mathcal F(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\}
\subset\mathbb C_{\mathcal Z}.                                        \qquad\text{(1)}
\]
We first prove \(\Theta_I(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\subseteq\mathcal T(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\).  Fix \(P\in\mathcal F(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\).  On \(\{A=a\}\), consistency and the definition \(\Delta=\mathbf 1\{C\leq T\}\) imply
\[
T(a)=\widetilde T+(T(a)-\widetilde T)\Delta.                            \qquad\text{(2)}
\]
Indeed, if \(\Delta=0\), then \(C>T(a)\) and \(\widetilde T=T(a)\); if \(\Delta=1\), (2) is tautological.  Conditional randomization, together with treatment overlap so that the arm conditional expectation is defined, now yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
E_P[T(a)\mid Z=z,R=r]
&=E_P[T(a)\mid A=a,Z=z,R=r]\\
&=b_{a,z}(r)+s^P_{a,z}(r).                                               \qquad\text{(3)}
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the second equality follows from (2), compatibility with \(P_{\mathrm{obs}}\), and the residual-contribution definition.  Subtracting (3) for \(a=0\) from (3) for \(a=1\) gives
\[
\tau_z^P(r)=b_{1,z}(r)-b_{0,z}(r)+s^P_{1,z}(r)-s^P_{0,z}(r).            \qquad\text{(4)}
\]

Bounded event time also gives, on \(\{A=a\}\),
\[
0\leq (T(a)-\widetilde T)\Delta
\leq(t_{\max}-\widetilde T)\Delta.                                    \qquad\text{(5)}
\]
Conditional expectation and the dropout-capacity definition therefore imply
\[
0\leq s^P_{a,z}(r)\leq u_{a,z}(r)                                      \qquad\text{(6)}
\]
for the conditional score law almost every \(r\).  The model-class restrictions make \(s^P_{a,z}\) \(L\)-Lipschitz and make \(u_{a,z}\) H\"older continuous.  Profile positivity makes the following conditional densities well defined, and Bayes' rule, treatment overlap, and the score-density bound give
\[
\frac{dP_{\mathrm{obs}}(R\in dr\mid A=a,Z=z)}{dr}
=\frac{\pi_a(z,r)p_z(r)}{P_{\mathrm{obs}}(A=a\mid Z=z)}
\geq\varepsilon c_p>0.                                                  \tag{7}
\]
A strict violation of either inequality in (6) at one point would, by continuity, persist on an interval having positive conditional probability by (7), contradicting (6) almost surely.  Thus (6) holds for every \(r\in[0,1]\).  Residual monotonicity and residual Lipschitz continuity then give
\[
s^P_{a,z}\in\mathcal S_{a,z}(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\qquad\text{for every }a,z. \qquad\text{(8)}
\]
Equations (4) and (8) prove the desired outer inclusion.

For the reverse inclusion, take any
\[
g=(b_{1,z}-b_{0,z}+f_{1,z}-f_{0,z})_{z\in\mathcal Z}
\in\mathcal T(P_{\mathrm{obs}}).
\]
The completion-witness lemma supplies a single full-data law \(P^f\in\mathcal F(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\) satisfying \(s^{P^f}_{a,z}=f_{a,z}\) simultaneously for every arm, profile, and score.  Equation (4), applied to \(P^f\), gives \(\tau^{P^f}=g\).  Hence
\[
\mathcal T(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\subseteq\Theta_I(P_{\mathrm{obs}}),
\]
which, together with the outer inclusion, proves law sharpness rather than only validity.

We finally establish the geometric assertions.  For fixed \((a,z)\), the zero function belongs to \(\mathcal S_{a,z}(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\), so the set is nonempty.  Its defining pointwise interval, monotonicity, and Lipschitz inequalities are preserved by convex combinations, so it is convex.  They are also preserved under uniform limits, so it is closed in \(C([0,1])\).  Moreover,
\[
\|f\|_\infty\leq\|u_{a,z}\|_\infty,
\qquad |f(r)-f(r')|\leq L|r-r'|.                                      \qquad\text{(9)}
\]
The first bound is finite because \(u_{a,z}\) is continuous on \([0,1]\).

For completeness, compactness follows directly from (9).  Given any sequence \((f_k)\) in the obstacle set, enumerate a countable dense subset of \([0,1]\).  At each dense point the scalar sequence is bounded.  Its convergent-subsequence extraction follows constructively by enclosing its values in a bounded interval, repeatedly retaining a half-interval containing infinitely many terms, and choosing increasing indices from the resulting nested intervals; their diameters tend to zero.  Repeating this extraction over the countable dense set and taking the diagonal subsequence produces a subsequence converging at every point of that dense set.  Given \(\epsilon>0\), choose a finite dense-subset net with mesh less than \(\epsilon/(3L)\).  Convergence on the finitely many net points and (9) imply, for all sufficiently large \(k,\ell\),
\[
\sup_{r\in[0,1]}|f_k(r)-f_\ell(r)|
\leq 2L\frac{\epsilon}{3L}+\frac{\epsilon}{3}=\epsilon.               \qquad\text{(10)}
\]
Thus the extracted subsequence is uniformly Cauchy, has a continuous uniform limit, and closedness puts that limit back in the obstacle set.  Every sequence therefore has a convergent subsequence; because the ambient norm topology is metric, \(\mathcal S_{a,z}(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\) is compact.

There are only \(2|\mathcal Z|\) obstacle factors, so their product is nonempty, compact, and convex.  The affine map
\[
(f_{a,z})_{a,z}\longmapsto
(b_{1,z}-b_{0,z}+f_{1,z}-f_{0,z})_{z\in\mathcal Z}                    \qquad\text{(11)}
\]
is continuous, since the sup-norm distance between two images is at most twice the largest sup-norm distance between their coordinates.  Its image is exactly \(\mathcal T(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\).  Continuous images preserve compactness, and affine images preserve convexity.  The image is nonempty because the product is nonempty.  This proves all claims.

Fix \(g\in\mathcal B(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\) and put
\[
d_z(r):=g_z(r)-b_{1,z}(r)+b_{0,z}(r).
\]
The pointwise-image definition is equivalent to
\[
-u_{0,z}(r)\leq d_z(r)\leq u_{1,z}(r)\qquad(z\in\mathcal Z,\ r\in[0,1]). \qquad\text{(1)}
\]
The proposed residuals are the positive and negative parts
\[
f^g_{1,z}=d_z^+,
\qquad f^g_{0,z}=(-d_z)^+.
\]
Because \(g_z,b_{1,z},b_{0,z}\) are continuous and the positive-part map is continuous, both residuals are continuous.  From (1), considering separately \(d_z\geq0\) and \(d_z<0\),
\[
0\leq f^g_{1,z}(r)\leq u_{1,z}(r),
\qquad
0\leq f^g_{0,z}(r)\leq u_{0,z}(r).                                    \qquad\text{(2)}
\]
Also,
\[
f^g_{1,z}(r)-f^g_{0,z}(r)=d_z(r).                                      \qquad\text{(3)}
\]

Equation (2) shows that \(q^g_{a,z}=f^g_{a,z}/u_{a,z}\) is a probability on \(\{u_{a,z}>0\}\).  On \(\{u_{a,z}=0\}\), (2) forces \(f^g_{a,z}=0\), so the stipulated value \(q^g_{a,z}=0\) is legal and, on both regions,
\[
q^g_{a,z}(r)u_{a,z}(r)=f^g_{a,z}(r).                                   \qquad\text{(4)}
\]

We verify the induced observation rather than assuming it.  For an armwise sampled record \((\widetilde T_a,\Delta_a)\), if \(\Delta_a=0\), then \(T(a)=\widetilde T_a<C(a)=t_{\max}+1\); if \(\Delta_a=1\), then \(C(a)=\widetilde T_a\leq T(a)\).  Therefore in either case
\[
\min\{T(a),C(a)\}=\widetilde T_a,
\qquad \mathbf 1\{C(a)\leq T(a)\}=\Delta_a.                          \qquad\text{(5)}
\]
Together with the observed marginal of \(X\), the observed conditional arm kernels, and the protocol treatment probabilities, (5) proves that the observed law under \(P^g_{\mathrm{cont}}\) is \(P_{\mathrm{obs}}\).  The construction draws treatment independently of both potential arm records given \(X\), gives consistency after setting \((T,C)=(T(A),C(A))\), and keeps \(T(a)\) in \([0,t_{\max}]\).

The same conditional calculation, now using (4), yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
s^{P^g_{\mathrm{cont}}}_{a,z}(r)
&=E[(T(a)-\widetilde T)\Delta\mid A=a,Z=z,R=r]\\
&=q^g_{a,z}(r)
E_{P_{\mathrm{obs}}}[(t_{\max}-\widetilde T)\Delta
 \mid A=a,Z=z,R=r]\\
&=q^g_{a,z}(r)u_{a,z}(r)
=f^g_{a,z}(r).                                                         \qquad\text{(6)}
\end{aligned}
\]
These residuals are continuous by (2), and no monotonicity or finite Lipschitz condition is required in the residual-continuity-only class.  All remaining overlap and observed-law regularity properties are inherited from \(P_{\mathrm{obs}}\).  Hence \(P^g_{\mathrm{cont}}\in\mathcal F_{\mathrm{cont}}(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\).

Finally, randomization, consistency, and the armwise decomposition of event time give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\tau_z^{P^g_{\mathrm{cont}}}(r)
&=b_{1,z}(r)-b_{0,z}(r)
 +f^g_{1,z}(r)-f^g_{0,z}(r)\\
&=b_{1,z}(r)-b_{0,z}(r)+d_z(r)
=g_z(r),                                                               \qquad\text{(7)}
\end{aligned}
\]
where (3) gives the second equality.  Thus one law attains the entire curve \(g\), including every zero-capacity contact.

Let
\[
\Theta_{I,\mathrm{cont}}(P_{\mathrm{obs}})
:=\{\tau^P:P\in\mathcal F_{\mathrm{cont}}(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\}.
\]
For any compatible residual-continuity-only law, bounded event time and the observation identity imply
\[
0\leq s^P_{a,z}(r)\leq u_{a,z}(r)                                     \qquad\text{(1)}
\]
first for the conditional score law almost every \(r\).  Profile positivity, Bayes' rule, treatment overlap, and the score-density bound imply
\[
\frac{dP_{\mathrm{obs}}(R\in dr\mid A=a,Z=z)}{dr}
=\frac{\pi_a(z,r)p_z(r)}{P_{\mathrm{obs}}(A=a\mid Z=z)}
\geq\varepsilon c_p>0.
\]
Because \(s^P_{a,z}\) and \(u_{a,z}\) are continuous, (1) therefore extends to every \(r\).  The causal arm decomposition gives
\[
b_{1,z}(r)-b_{0,z}(r)-u_{0,z}(r)
\leq\tau_z^P(r)\leq
b_{1,z}(r)-b_{0,z}(r)+u_{1,z}(r).                                      \qquad\text{(2)}
\]
Moreover \(\tau^P\) is continuous, because the observed base functions are H\"older continuous and the residuals are continuous.  Hence \(\Theta_{I,\mathrm{cont}}(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\subseteq\mathcal B(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\).  Conversely, the continuous-box completion lemma constructs, for every \(g\in\mathcal B(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\), a single \(P^g_{\mathrm{cont}}\in\mathcal F_{\mathrm{cont}}(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\) with \(\tau^{P^g_{\mathrm{cont}}}=g\).  Thus
\[
\Theta_{I,\mathrm{cont}}(P_{\mathrm{obs}})=\mathcal B(P_{\mathrm{obs}}). \qquad\text{(3)}
\]
At a fixed \((z,r)\), the two continuous choices obtained by taking the residual difference everywhere equal to \(u_{1,z}\) or to \(-u_{0,z}\), and their convex mixtures, show that the projection in (2) is the full displayed interval, not merely an outer interval.

We next verify the comparison with the published conservative endpoints.  Introduce, only for this calculation,
\[
\xi_{a,z}(r):=P_{\mathrm{obs}}(\Delta=1\mid A=a,Z=z,R=r),
\qquad
\nu_{\delta,a,z}(r):=E_{P_{\mathrm{obs}}}[\widetilde T
 \mid\Delta=\delta,A=a,Z=z,R=r].
\]
The law of total expectation and the two observed-base definitions give
\[
b_{a,z}(r)=\nu_{0,a,z}(r)\{1-\xi_{a,z}(r)\}
            +\nu_{1,a,z}(r)\xi_{a,z}(r),                               \qquad\text{(4)}
\]
whereas the dropout-capacity definition gives
\[
u_{a,z}(r)=\{t_{\max}-\nu_{1,a,z}(r)\}\xi_{a,z}(r).                    \qquad\text{(5)}
\]
Consequently
\[
b_{a,z}(r)+u_{a,z}(r)
=\nu_{0,a,z}(r)\{1-\xi_{a,z}(r)\}+t_{\max}\xi_{a,z}(r).               \qquad\text{(6)}
\]
The cited conservative-endpoint result of Wang et al. identifies (4) as its lower arm endpoint, (6) as its conservative upper arm endpoint, and forms CATE endpoints by subtracting opposite arm endpoints.  Those subtractions are exactly
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{1,z}-(b_{0,z}+u_{0,z})&=b_{1,z}-b_{0,z}-u_{0,z},\\
(b_{1,z}+u_{1,z})-b_{0,z}&=b_{1,z}-b_{0,z}+u_{1,z},                     \qquad\text{(7)}
\end{aligned}
\]
which proves the stated estimand-level correspondence with (2).

For the maintained monotone-Lipschitz class, every \(g\in\mathcal T(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\) has
\[
g_z-(b_{1,z}-b_{0,z})=f_{1,z}-f_{0,z}
\quad\text{with}\quad 0\leq f_{a,z}\leq u_{a,z}.
\]
Therefore \(-u_{0,z}\leq f_{1,z}-f_{0,z}\leq u_{1,z}\), proving
\[
\mathcal T(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\subseteq\mathcal B(P_{\mathrm{obs}}).    \qquad\text{(8)}
\]

It remains to prove the advertised strictness certificate.  Suppose that for some \(z\) and \(r_1<r_2\),
\[
u_{1,z}(r_1)+u_{0,z}(r_2)>2L(r_2-r_1).                                 \qquad\text{(9)}
\]
Define a continuous switch
\[
\lambda(r)=
\begin{cases}
0,&r\leq r_1,\\
(r-r_1)/(r_2-r_1),&r_1<r<r_2,\\
1,&r\geq r_2,
\end{cases}
\]
and, for the profile in (9), define
\[
d_z(r)=\{1-\lambda(r)\}u_{1,z}(r)-\lambda(r)u_{0,z}(r).                \qquad\text{(10)}
\]
For every other profile \(z'\), set \(d_{z'}=0\), and set
\[
g_{z'}=b_{1,z'}-b_{0,z'}+d_{z'}.
\]
Because (10) is a convex combination of the two continuous endpoint functions \(u_{1,z}\) and \(-u_{0,z}\),
\[
-u_{0,z}(r)\leq d_z(r)\leq u_{1,z}(r)
\]
for every \(r\); the same inequality is immediate for \(d_{z'}=0\).  Hence \(g\in\mathcal B(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\).  But (10) gives
\[
d_z(r_1)=u_{1,z}(r_1),
\qquad d_z(r_2)=-u_{0,z}(r_2),
\]
so (9) implies
\[
|d_z(r_2)-d_z(r_1)|>2L(r_2-r_1).                                      \qquad\text{(11)}
\]
If \(g\) belonged to \(\mathcal T(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\), then \(d_z=f_{1,z}-f_{0,z}\) for two \(L\)-Lipschitz obstacle functions.  The triangle inequality would instead give
\[
|d_z(r_2)-d_z(r_1)|
\leq |f_{1,z}(r_2)-f_{1,z}(r_1)|
   + |f_{0,z}(r_2)-f_{0,z}(r_1)|
\leq 2L(r_2-r_1),
\]
contradicting (11).  Thus \(g\in\mathcal B(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\setminus\mathcal T(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\), and the inclusion in (8) is strict under the observed criterion.

added_lemmas.statement: Under the causal conditions of Wang et al., their conservative post-dropout formula has arm-specific lower endpoint \(E_{P_{\mathrm{obs}}}[\widetilde T\mid A=a,Z=z,R=r]\) and upper endpoint \(E_{P_{\mathrm{obs}}}[\widetilde T\mathbf 1\{\Delta=0\}+t_{\max}\mathbf 1\{\Delta=1\}\mid A=a,Z=z,R=r]\); the CATE lower endpoint subtracts the control-arm upper endpoint from the treated-arm lower endpoint, and the CATE upper endpoint subtracts the control-arm lower endpoint from the treated-arm upper endpoint.

source.locator: Equation (4), equation (8), and Theorem 5.1 with equation (9) in arXiv:2510.13397v3, pages 5--6 of the PDF

attestation.note: Transcribed from the displayed formulas at the cited locations in version 3 of the source PDF.

proposed.statement: For every family \(f=(f_{a,z})\) with \(f_{a,z}\in\mathcal S_{a,z}(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\), the constructed law \(P^f\) belongs to \(\mathcal F(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\), has residual contribution \(s_{a,z}^{P^f}=f_{a,z}\), and preserves the observed censoring law. On \(\{u_{a,z}>0\}\), attainability follows from \(E[(T(a)-\widetilde T)\Delta\mid a,z,r]=q_{a,z}(r)u_{a,z}(r)=f_{a,z}(r)\); on \(\{u_{a,z}=0\}\), feasibility forces \(f_{a,z}=0\), and the tie convention keeps the completion legal.
proposed.justification: This is the attainability step that turns valid inequalities into law sharpness, including zero-capacity contacts.
proposed.gap: Wang et al. prove endpoint validity in Theorem 5.1 and Appendix D.2 but do not construct one full-data completion attaining an entire shape-coupled curve.
proposed.consumer: It lets trial analysts interpret every reported curve in the set as arising from an observationally equivalent informative-dropout law.

proposed_core_edits.reason: Declare every maintained restriction checked directly in the full-law membership proof; the mathematical claim is unchanged.

proposed.statement: The identified set of profile-specific CATE curves is exactly \(\{\tau^P:P\in\mathcal F(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\}=\mathcal T(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\). The set \(\mathcal T(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\) is nonempty, compact, and convex in \(\mathbb C_{\mathcal Z}\).
proposed.justification: The theorem replaces unrelated pointwise intervals by the joint law-sharp function-valued causal object.
proposed.gap: Beresteanu, Molchanov, and Molinari characterize random-set expectations abstractly, while Wang et al. give only covariatewise survival-CATE endpoints; neither identifies this dropout obstacle image.
proposed.consumer: The sharp compact set is the target needed for honest sign statements along a prognostic score and across genomic profiles.

proposed_core_edits.reason: Declare the observed-base, dropout-capacity, and residual-contribution definitions used directly in the outer-bound and CATE-decomposition steps; the mathematical claim is unchanged.

proposed.statement: For every \(g\in\mathcal B(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\), the constructed law \(P^g_{\mathrm{cont}}\) belongs to \(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{cont}}(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\), preserves the observed law, and satisfies \(\tau^{P^g_{\mathrm{cont}}}=g\). In particular, \(f^g_{1,z}=[g_z-b_{1,z}+b_{0,z}]_+\) and \(f^g_{0,z}=[-g_z+b_{1,z}-b_{0,z}]_+\) are continuous, obey \(0\le f^g_{a,z}\le u_{a,z}\), and the ratio completion is legal on both \(\{u_{a,z}>0\}\) and \(\{u_{a,z}=0\}\).
proposed.justification: This separate attainability result prevents the residual-continuity benchmark from borrowing membership in the monotone-Lipschitz law class.
proposed.gap: Wang et al. establish validity of covariatewise endpoints but do not construct a single residual-continuous full-data law for every curve in the continuous endpoint image.
proposed.consumer: It certifies the exact benchmark against which the contraction produced by the clinically calibrated shape restrictions is measured.

proposed_core_edits.reason: Declare the dropout-capacity and residual-contribution definitions used directly by the ratio-completion calculation; the mathematical claim is unchanged.

proposed.statement: For the separately defined residual-continuity-only compatible-law class, \(\{\tau^P:P\in\mathcal F_{\mathrm{cont}}(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\}=\mathcal B(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\subset\mathbb C_{\mathcal Z}\). Its coordinate interval is \([b_{1,z}(r)-b_{0,z}(r)-u_{0,z}(r),b_{1,z}(r)-b_{0,z}(r)+u_{1,z}(r)]\), the continuous-curve image of the conservative endpoint formula in Wang et al., Theorem 5.1 and equations (8)--(9). For the maintained monotone-Lipschitz class, \(\mathcal T(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\subseteq\mathcal B(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\). A sufficient observed criterion for strict inclusion is the existence of \(z,r_1<r_2\) such that \(u_{1,z}(r_1)+u_{0,z}(r_2)>2L(r_2-r_1)\), because the two endpoint choices permitted by \(\mathcal B(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\) violate the \(2L\)-Lipschitz restriction on \(f_{1,z}-f_{0,z}\).
proposed.justification: The result gives a valid continuous-function sanity reduction and an observable sufficient certificate that curve coupling strictly improves on pointwise bounds.
proposed.gap: Wang et al.'s endpoint theorem permits independent adversarial completions at each score value and supplies no observed sufficient criterion certifying that joint residual shape strictly contracts its product region.
proposed.consumer: The sufficient condition identifies profiles and score pairs for which defending the residual-shape sensitivity model can change a treatment-benefit conclusion.

proposed_core_edits.reason: Add the theorem-granularity published premise that supports the Wang et al. endpoint attribution; the mathematical claim is unchanged.

proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(v\in\mathbb B_*\).  All the integrals below are finite: each
\(v_z\) has finite total variation, while the functions \(b_{a,z}\) and
every member of \(\mathcal S_{a,z}(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\) are continuous on
the compact interval \([0,1]\).  By the definitions of the sharp curve
set and its support function,
\[
\begin{aligned}
h_{\mathcal T}(v)
&=\sup_{\substack{f_{a,z}\in\mathcal S_{a,z}(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\\
                   a\in\{0,1\},\ z\in\mathcal Z}}
 \sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}\int
 \{b_{1,z}-b_{0,z}+f_{1,z}-f_{0,z}\}\,dv_z \\
&=\sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}\int(b_{1,z}-b_{0,z})\,dv_z
  +\sup_{(f_{a,z})}\sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}
       \left\{\int f_{1,z}\,dv_z+\int f_{0,z}\,d(-v_z)\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The feasible family is a finite Cartesian product of nonempty sets, because
the zero function belongs to every obstacle set.  Consequently the last
supremum is the sum of the coordinatewise suprema: the inequality from left
to right is immediate, and the reverse inequality follows by choosing, for
each of the finitely many coordinates, a feasible function within
\(\epsilon/(2|\mathcal Z|)\) of its supremum and then sending
\(\epsilon\downarrow0\).  The definition of \(V_{a,z}\) therefore gives
\[
h_{\mathcal T}(v)
=\sum_z\int(b_{1,z}-b_{0,z})\,dv_z
 +\sum_z\{V_{1,z}(v_z;u)+V_{0,z}(-v_z;u)\}.
\]
This proves the continuous support decomposition.

Fix now one arm-profile pair \((a,z)\), put
\(w_j=\int\phi_{j,h}\,dv_z\), and put
\(\bar u_j=[u_{a,z}(r_j)-Mh^\beta]_+\).  Linearity of integration and the
definition of \(\Phi_h\) yield
\[
 \int\Phi_hx\,dv_z=\sum_{j=0}^m w_jx_j.
\]
Thus the grid support problem is the finite linear program
\[
 p^*=\max_x\left\{\sum_{j=0}^m w_jx_j:
 0\le x_j\le\bar u_j,\quad
 0\le x_{j+1}-x_j\le Lh\ (0\le j<m)\right\}.
\]
Its feasible polytope is nonempty, since it contains \(x=0\), and compact,
since \(0\le x_j\le\bar u_j<\infty\).  Hence it has a maximizer \(x^*\).

For completeness, we derive the specialized dual equality.  Write the four
families of inequalities as
\[
 x_j-\bar u_j\le0,\qquad -x_j\le0,\qquad
 x_{j+1}-x_j-Lh\le0,\qquad x_j-x_{j+1}\le0.
\]
At \(x^*\), the vector \(w=(w_0,\ldots,w_m)\) is a nonnegative linear
combination of the normals of the active inequalities.  Indeed, if it were
not, finite-dimensional separation from the finitely generated cone of
active normals would give a vector \(y\) whose inner product with every
active normal is nonpositive but with \(w^Ty>0\).  Every inactive inequality
has strictly positive slack, so \(x^*+ty\) would remain feasible for all
sufficiently small \(t>0\), contradicting
\(w^T(x^*+ty)>w^Tx^*\).  Denote the resulting nonnegative coefficients by
\(\lambda_j^+,\lambda_j^-,g_j,d_j\), in the order displayed above, and
extend the arc variables by
\(g_{-1}=g_m=d_{-1}=d_m=0\).  Equating the coefficient of \(x_j\) gives
\[
 \lambda_j^+-\lambda_j^-+g_{j-1}-g_j+d_j-d_{j-1}=w_j,
 \qquad j=0,\ldots,m.
\]
Hence \(d_h=(\lambda^+,\lambda^-,g,d)\) belongs to
\(\mathcal D_h(w,\bar u)\).  Because a multiplier can be positive only for
an active constraint,
\[
\begin{aligned}
p^*=w^Tx^*
 &=\sum_{j=0}^m\bar u_j\lambda_j^+
   +Lh\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}g_j.
\end{aligned}
\]
Conversely, for every primal-feasible \(x\) and every
\(d_h\in\mathcal D_h(w,\bar u)\), the balance equations imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_jw_jx_j
&=\sum_j(\lambda_j^+-\lambda_j^-)x_j
 +\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}g_j(x_{j+1}-x_j)
 +\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}d_j(x_j-x_{j+1})\\
&\le \sum_j\bar u_j\lambda_j^+
       +Lh\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}g_j,
\end{aligned}
\]
using respectively \(x_j\le\bar u_j\), \(x_j\ge0\),
\(x_{j+1}-x_j\le Lh\), and \(x_{j+1}-x_j\ge0\).  This is weak duality;
the multipliers constructed at \(x^*\) attain equality, proving the displayed
minimum formula.

The same equations are node-balance equations on the path
\(0,1,\ldots,m\): \(g_j\) and \(d_j\) are the two oriented arc flows, while
\(\lambda_j^+\) and \(\lambda_j^-\) are nonnegative node transactions.
The only nonzero arc capacity cost is \(Lh\sum_jg_j\), and the upper-obstacle
transactions cost \(\sum_j\bar u_j\lambda_j^+\).  A feasible primal vector
and feasible dual flow with the common displayed objective are therefore a
finite, directly checkable min-cost-transshipment certificate.

Set \(\delta_h=Mh^\beta\).  We first verify the inner inclusion one
arm-profile pair at a time.  Let \(\Phi_hx\in\mathcal S^h_{a,z}\).  On each
interval \([r_j,r_{j+1}]\), its slope is
\((x_{j+1}-x_j)/h\in[0,L]\).  Hence \(\Phi_hx\) is nonnegative,
nondecreasing, and \(L\)-Lipschitz.  If
\(r\in[r_j,r_{j+1}]\) and \(k\in\{j,j+1\}\), the H\"older condition on
\(u_{a,z}\) gives
\[
 u_{a,z}(r)\ge u_{a,z}(r_k)-M|r-r_k|^\beta
             \ge u_{a,z}(r_k)-\delta_h.
\]
Because \(u_{a,z}(r)\ge0\), this implies
\[
 x_k\le [u_{a,z}(r_k)-\delta_h]_+\le u_{a,z}(r).
\]
The interpolant is a convex combination of \(x_j\) and \(x_{j+1}\), so
\(\Phi_hx(r)\le u_{a,z}(r)\).  All defining obstacle inequalities therefore
hold, proving
\(\mathcal S^h_{a,z}\subseteq\mathcal S_{a,z}(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\).
Taking the finite product over \((a,z)\) and then applying the affine map in
the definition of the curve sets proves
\[
 \mathcal T_h(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\subseteq\mathcal T(P_{\mathrm{obs}}).
\]

For the reverse approximation, fix
\(f\in\mathcal S_{a,z}(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\) and define the nodal vector
\[
 x_j=[f(r_j)-\delta_h]_+,
 \qquad j=0,\ldots,m.
\]
Since \(f(r_j)\le u_{a,z}(r_j)\),
\(x_j\le[u_{a,z}(r_j)-\delta_h]_+\).  The map
\(q(t)=[t-\delta_h]_+\) is nondecreasing and one-Lipschitz.  The monotonicity
and Lipschitz restrictions on \(f\) therefore imply
\[
 0\le x_{j+1}-x_j
 \le f(r_{j+1})-f(r_j)
 \le Lh.
\]
Thus \(\Phi_hx\in\mathcal S^h_{a,z}\).  Moreover,
\(|f(r_j)-x_j|\le\delta_h\) at every node.  Writing
\(r=(1-t)r_j+tr_{j+1}\), \(0\le t\le1\), and using the
\(L\)-Lipschitz property twice gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left|f(r)-\{(1-t)f(r_j)+tf(r_{j+1})\}\right|
&\le(1-t)Lth+tL(1-t)h\\
&=2t(1-t)Lh\le Lh.
\end{aligned}
\]
The nodal clipping contributes at most \(\delta_h\), whence
\[
 \|f-\Phi_hx\|_\infty\le Lh+Mh^\beta.
\]

Now take any
\(g=(b_{1,z}-b_{0,z}+f_{1,z}-f_{0,z})_z\in\mathcal T(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\).
Apply the preceding construction separately to every \(f_{a,z}\), obtaining
\(f^h_{a,z}\in\mathcal S^h_{a,z}\), and define
\(g^h=(b_{1,z}-b_{0,z}+f^h_{1,z}-f^h_{0,z})_z\).  Then
\(g^h\in\mathcal T_h(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\) and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|g-g^h\|_\infty
&\le\max_z\left(
 \|f_{1,z}-f^h_{1,z}\|_\infty+
 \|f_{0,z}-f^h_{0,z}\|_\infty\right)\\
&\le2(Lh+Mh^\beta).
\end{aligned}
\]
The inner inclusion makes the directed distance from
\(\mathcal T_h(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\) to \(\mathcal T(P_{\mathrm{obs}})\)
zero, and the last display bounds the opposite directed distance.  Their
maximum is the asserted Hausdorff bound.  Every inequality used only the
common constants \(L,M,\beta\), so the bound is uniform over
\(P\in\mathfrak P\).  The proof never divides by \(u_{a,z}\) and the clipping
map is valid when its argument is zero; hence intervals and isolated points
on which \(u_{a,z}=0\) require no separate positivity condition.

Let \(E=\mathbb C_{\mathcal Z,h_n}\) with its inherited norm, and write
\(B_E=\{x\in E:\|x\|\le1\}\).  We first establish directly the support
representation of Hausdorff distance needed here.  If
\(d=d_H(K_1,K_2)\), then
\(K_1\subseteq K_2+dB_E\) and \(K_2\subseteq K_1+dB_E\).  Therefore, for
every \(v\in E^*\),
\[
 |h_{K_1}(v)-h_{K_2}(v)|\le d\|v\|_*.
\]
Conversely, put
\[
 q=\sup_{\|v\|_*\le1}|h_{K_1}(v)-h_{K_2}(v)|.
\]
If some \(x\in K_1\) were outside the closed convex set \(K_2+qB_E\),
finite-dimensional separation would give a nonzero \(v\in E^*\) such that
\[
 v(x)>h_{K_2+qB_E}(v)=h_{K_2}(v)+q\|v\|_*.
\]
After division by \(\|v\|_*\), this contradicts the definition of \(q\).
Thus \(K_1\subseteq K_2+qB_E\); interchanging the sets gives the reverse
inclusion.  It follows that
\[
 d_H(K_1,K_2)=
 \sup_{\|v\|_*\le1}|h_{K_1}(v)-h_{K_2}(v)|.
\]

For any set \(K\) contained in the closed radius-\(\mathsf R\) ball and any
\(v,d\in E^*\),
\[
 |h_K(v)-h_K(d)|
 \le\sup_{x\in K}|(v-d)(x)|
 \le\mathsf R\|v-d\|_*.
\]
Given \(v\) in the dual unit ball, the definition of the
\(\delta_n\)-net supplies \(d\in\mathcal D_n\) with
\(\|v-d\|_*\le\delta_n\).  Applying the preceding Lipschitz bound to both
sets yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
|h_{K_1}(v)-h_{K_2}(v)|
&\le |h_{K_1}(d)-h_{K_2}(d)|
   +|h_{K_1}(v)-h_{K_1}(d)|
   +|h_{K_2}(v)-h_{K_2}(d)|\\
&\le \max_{e\in\mathcal D_n}|h_{K_1}(e)-h_{K_2}(e)|
   +2\mathsf R\delta_n.
\end{aligned}
\]
Taking the supremum over the dual unit ball and using the established
support representation proves the claim.

open_obligations.what_is_open: The missing step is a band-subclass-uniform asymptotic linearization that links the declared score class to the gridded support values, baseline-law constraints, and optimized leaf endpoints through changing optimal faces, followed by conditional validity of the one-common-multiplier critical value for that linked process.
open_obligations.obstruction: The frozen score assumptions impose only centering, an envelope moment bound, and an entropy bound. They define neither the statistics represented by the scores nor a uniform remainder or multiplier coupling. The admissible zero-score class satisfies every stated score condition but has multiplier critical value zero and cannot control a nondegenerate eligible-leaf mass error; thus the desired multiplier/leaf conclusion is not derivable from the declared primitives.
open_obligations.attempted: I derived a contact-set-uniform contraction of each obstacle by positive-part shifting and used it with the external nuisance band and the grid theorem. This closes the robust whole-set geometry without differentiating active faces. I then attempted to calibrate the baseline-law and leaf projections from the stated score process, but there is no declared score-to-statistic equation to which the moment and entropy controls can be applied; the zero-score witness confirms that this is not recoverable by empirical-process algebra alone.
open_obligations.partial_result:
The changing-contact geometry itself admits the following uniform bound.
For two nonnegative capacities \(u,u'\), set
\(\rho=\|u-u'\|_\infty\).  If \(f\in\mathcal S(u)\), define
\(C_\rho f=(f-\rho)_+\).  The positive-part map is nondecreasing and
one-Lipschitz, so \(C_\rho f\) remains nonnegative, nondecreasing, and
\(L\)-Lipschitz.  Since \(f\le u\le u'+\rho\), one also has
\(C_\rho f\le u'\), and
\(\|f-C_\rho f\|_\infty\le\rho\).  Interchanging \(u,u'\) proves
\[
 d_H\{\mathcal S(u),\mathcal S(u')\}\le\|u-u'\|_\infty,
\]
with no condition on either zero-capacity contact set.  Consequently, if
\(\rho_b=\max_{a,z}\|b_{a,z}-b'_{a,z}\|_\infty\) and
\(\rho_u=\max_{a,z}\|u_{a,z}-u'_{a,z}\|_\infty\), applying
\(C_{\rho_u}\) separately in the two arms gives
\[
 d_H\{\mathcal T(b,u),\mathcal T(b',u')\}
 \le2\rho_b+2\rho_u.
\]
On the event in the external-band prerequisite, every admissible nuisance
element in the band is within \(2r_n\) of the true nuisance.  Hence the
closure of the union of its admissible obstacle images is within
\(8r_n\) of the true curve set.  Expanding each gridded image by
\(2(Lh_n+Mh_n^\beta)\), as justified by the grid theorem, gives an observable
robust-band whole-set superset that contains the true curve set on that event
and whose directed excess is at most
\(8r_n+2(Lh_n+Mh_n^\beta)\), before any optional direction-net remainder.
Thus changing and even newly appearing contact sets do not obstruct the
whole-set rate.

What remains unproved is the simultaneous multiplier and leaf projection
part.  The current premises bound only the envelope, moment, and covering
numbers of \(\Psi_n\); no declared equation connects an element of
\(\Psi_n\) to the estimation error of a support value, a leaf numerator, a
leaf mass, or an endpoint optimizer, and no premise asserts a uniform
linearization remainder or conditional multiplier coupling.  This is a
logical, not merely technical, omission.  For example, take the score class
to consist of the zero function for every index in
\(\mathcal D_n\times\mathcal G_n\).  It is centered, has zero envelope
moment, and has covering number one, so all three stated score conditions
hold.  Nevertheless, for an eligible leaf \(G\) with \(P_X(G)=1/2\) and an
odd sample size \(n\), the empirical leaf mass cannot equal \(1/2\), whereas
the multiplier supremum of the zero score class and its critical value are
identically zero.  Hence the declared score conditions alone do not control
even the leaf-mass error, much less the optimized leaf endpoints.  A complete
positive theorem must first define the support and leaf statistics and prove
a band-subclass-uniform score expansion for them, including the optimizer's
changing critical cone, and must then establish conditional multiplier
quantile validity for that expansion.  Neither required link is a consequence
of the frozen premises.
